evidence.claim: Follow the Mississippi from Twain’s Hannibal to French houses and earthquake country.
evidence.quote: From the humble beginnings of Mark Twain in Hannibal to the soaring majesty of the St. Louis Arch, the Missouri Great River Road spans a broad range of American culture.

evidence.claim: Missouri’s Great River Road follows a Mississippi corridor of river towns, St. Louis city life and French heritage at Ste. Genevieve.
evidence.quote: Variety is what you’ll find as you travel this scenic stretch of the Mississippi River. Take in the rich city life of St. Louis

evidence.claim: The Mississippi River Parkway Commission presents the drive through its cultural variety, from Mark Twain’s Hannibal to the St. Louis Arch and the earthquake history of New Madrid.

evidence.claim: The Mississippi County, Arkansas Road Improvement District erected it in 1924 after paving the North–South Road, already a major route between St. Louis and Memphis.
evidence.quote: At the time, the highway was called the North–South Road, and it was already a major route between St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee;

evidence.claim: That arch now crosses U.S. 61 at the Missouri–Arkansas line, with a different state greeting on each side.
evidence.quote: The concrete horseshoe arch reads "Entering Arkansas" on one side and "Entering Missouri" on the other.

evidence.quote: U.S. Route 61 runs along Holland's southern boundary, connecting the city with Steele to the northeast and Blytheville, Arkansas, to the south.

evidence.claim: French heritage at Ste. Genevieve.
evidence.quote: Discover the rich French heritage of places like Ste. Genevieve.

evidence.claim: Hannibal supplied Mark Twain with childhood settings for The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.
evidence.quote: Twain drew from his childhood settings for his novels The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884).

evidence.claim: Mark Twain Cave inspired the episode in which Tom and Becky become lost.
evidence.quote: Mark Twain Cave - The cave that inspired Twain's tale of a lost Tom & Becky.

evidence.claim: The town also commemorated its writer with a lighthouse, built in 1933 as a public works project under Franklin D. Roosevelt.
evidence.quote: The Mark Twain Memorial Lighthouse was constructed in 1933 as a public works project under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

evidence.claim: Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy and Bill Clinton each lit it on ceremonial occasions.
evidence.quote: It has been lit on ceremonial occasions at three separate times by Presidents Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy, and Bill Clinton.

evidence.claim: For a view of the landscape behind the fiction, Lover’s Leap overlooks both downtown Hannibal and the Mississippi River.
evidence.quote: Lover's Leap - Cliffside overlooking the Mississippi River and downtown Hannibal.

evidence.claim: The flood of 1785 sent Ste. Genevieve to a new location two miles north and about half a mile inland.
evidence.quote: Following the great flood of 1785, the town moved from its initial location on the floodplain of the Mississippi River, to its present location two miles north and about a half mile inland.

evidence.claim: Louis Bolduc salvaged parts of his damaged riverfront house and incorporated them into a larger house built in 1792–1793.
evidence.quote: Bolduc incorporated these materials into his new and larger house, built in 1792–1793.

evidence.claim: Among the town’s oldest surviving buildings are houses with upright wooden posts, either planted in the earth or set on a raised foundation.
evidence.quote: Walls of buildings were built based on wood "posts" either dug into the ground (poteaux en terre) or set on a raised stone or brick foundation (poteaux sur solle).

evidence.claim: In the posts-in-the-ground houses, separate stone pillars support the floor.
evidence.quote: The floor is supported by separate stone pillars.

evidence.claim: Three of the nation’s five surviving examples stand in Ste. Genevieve.
evidence.quote: Three of the five surviving poteaux en terre houses in the nation are in Ste. Genevieve.

evidence.claim: Louis Bolduc salvaged parts of his damaged riverfront house
evidence.quote: Although much of the house was severely damaged by flooding, parts were dismantled and moved north

evidence.claim: New Madrid sits on the north side of Kentucky Bend, where the Mississippi makes an oxbow around a piece of Kentucky.
evidence.quote: The town is on the north side of the Kentucky Bend in the Mississippi River, which is also known as "New Madrid Bend" or "Madrid Bend." The river curves in an oxbow around an exclave of Fulton County, Kentucky.

evidence.claim: On February 7, 1812, an earthquake destroyed the town.
evidence.quote: February 7, 1812, 09:45 UTC (03:45 am local time): M 7.4–8.6, epicenter near New Madrid, Missouri. The town of New Madrid was destroyed.

evidence.claim: Uplift along the Reelfoot Fault produced temporary waterfalls at the bend and waves that traveled upstream.
evidence.quote: Uplift along a segment of this reverse fault created temporary waterfalls on the Mississippi at Kentucky Bend, created waves that propagated upstream,

evidence.claim: Across the region, the earthquakes collapsed riverbanks, destroyed sandbars and made some islands disappear.
evidence.quote: Waves on the Mississippi River caused boats to wash ashore; river banks rose, sand bars were destroyed, and some islands completely disappeared.

evidence.claim: The New Madrid Historical Museum interprets the southern Missouri earthquakes of 1811 and 1812.
evidence.quote: Learn about the earthquakes that rocked southern Missouri in 1811 and 1812 at the New Madrid Historical Museum.

evidence.claim: The Mark Twain Boyhood Home & Museum marked its centennial in 2012.
evidence.quote: The Mark Twain Boyhood Home & Museum marked its 100th anniversary in 2012;

evidence.claim: Posts set partly in dirt left these walls vulnerable to floods, termites and rot, even as stone pillars carried the floors.
evidence.quote: As the wooden posts were partially set into dirt, the walls of such buildings were extremely vulnerable to flood damage, termites and rot.

evidence.claim: The sequence began in December 1811, followed by further major earthquakes in January and February 1812.
evidence.quote: beginning with an initial earthquake of moment magnitude 7.2–8.2 on December 16, 1811, followed by a moment magnitude 7.4 aftershock on the same day. Two additional earthquakes of similar magnitude followed in January and February 1812.

evidence.claim: collapsed riverbanks
evidence.quote: Subsidence, uplift, fissures, landslides and riverbank collapses were common.

evidence.claim: Reelfoot Fault
evidence.quote: This shock was definitively attributed to the Reelfoot Fault by Johnston and Schweig.

evidence.claim: At Cape Girardeau, the downtown floodwall carries a 24-panel mural, with Riverfront Park and views of the Mississippi behind it.
evidence.quote: The largest is the Mississippi River Tales Mural, located on the city's downtown floodwall.

evidence.claim: a 24-panel mural
evidence.quote: features 24 panels.

evidence.claim: with Riverfront Park and views of the Mississippi behind it.
evidence.quote: Behind the floodwall lies the Riverfront Park of Cape Girardeau Missouri, where riverboats dock and visitors can view the Mississippi River.
